analysis.title: If This Was A Normal Week…
key_insights: Tchir calls last week abnormal: price action was driven by supply (bonds, energy, chips), stop losses across markets, and thin real liquidity ("faux liquidity"), not by the usual data or politics.

US political news (a partial waiver of the Russia/Iran sanctions act within a month of signing, Musk joining the push against Zelensky, a Greenland oil post) did not visibly move markets. He thinks it is still a background factor that makes a recovery harder for risk takers.

Diesel: the Russian diesel deal was too small to matter. The IEA/EU release is about 20 million barrels pulled forward from the March-agreed reserves, not 50 million new barrels, and depends on each government meeting its quota. A diesel export ban would be a mistake and the administration backed off it.

The quickest relief for fuel prices would be a Middle East resolution. Oil is leaving the region but there is no evidence distillates are. The US blockade on Iranian shipping is working but keeps energy prices high. A Ukraine-Russia refinery-strike ceasefire would only have a second-order effect on global energy prices.

He is not optimistic on a big near-term drop in energy prices and warns against being too bullish on the commodities themselves. Owning global energy producers remains his main focus, expecting a sell-off after any resolution.
He says the world is moving to ProSec (Production for Security) and that after the midterms US steps on ProSec will be discussed regardless of outcome.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.4% to 5.35% over three months in a steady grind, then fell 17 bps this week. He attributes the drop mainly to hope or fear that compute-related debt issuance will slow, plus positioning and a pause in corporate issuance, not data, the Fed or the deficit.
German vs French and Italian 2-year spreads widened 50 bps in two days. He says the news only catalyzed a view, and the move tested thin liquidity and complacent positioning.

The MOVE index sat near its March peak while the VIX was well below its yearly average. The VIX moved Thursday and Friday but closed well below June/July levels and below 30. He calls the VIX a poor predictor because vol-selling income strategies suppress it.

JEPQ and JEPI hold about $90B combined, and other vol-selling equity ETFs (QQQI, SPYI, QYLD, DIVO, GPIQ, GPIX) add roughly $100B. He asks whether they can keep suppressing vol or will be forced to cover, which could drive a much larger vol rise.

Credit ETFs (HYG, JNK, LQD, VCSH, JAAA) trade near NAV. JBBB and ANGL trade at slight discounts. CDX trades slightly tighter than its Bloomberg intrinsic value, which is not a source of reinforcing widening, though he doubts the calculation.

He expects the "orderly" spread widening to turn "fast and furious". Dealers are pulling back on liquidity, and he wants to see whether a $25 million block of 1-2 week old new issues can be sold on the wire.

He is as cautious on corporate credit as in a long time. This is about positioning and untested liquidity, not credit quality. A test could mean 10-20 bps wider on IG and 3-5 points on HY, and he sees a large fast move down as likelier than a big tightening.

On equities he is very cautious. Equities held up through rising yields, but he expects them to struggle with rising spreads, especially in the compute-spend sectors that drive returns and the economy.

Leveraged ETF positioning is aggressively bullish: TQQQ is about $34B vs SQQQ about $2.2B, and Nasdaq 100 leveraged ETFs total near $60B. SOXL is about $22B, with SOX and USD adding about $5B. NVDL holds about $4B on NVDA, and MUU is about the same size. He sees mechanical buying and selling risk in top-heavy indices.

His main scenario is a credit and equity sell-off that starts with wider compute-related spreads. Compute equities fall because their valuations depend on the buildout, and other spreads widen on positioning. The sell-off then continues even if compute spreads tighten, because investors worry about capital access and the economy. He admits this needs unusual steps to work.

Compute equities and credit are the likely starting point of a sell-off, because valuations depend on the spending buildout and debt issuance.
Tchir is as cautious as in a long time because of positioning and liquidity. He sees 10-20 bps of widening on IG and 3-5 points on HY.

risk_factors: Faux liquidity in credit and equities, with positioning too complacent.
Vol-selling ETFs being forced to cover, or stop losses cascading.
Slower compute-related debt issuance, and wider compute credit spreads leading to equity declines.
European sovereign credit stress (France, Italy, Spain vs Germany).
Mechanical flows from leveraged ETFs and top-heavy indices (Nasdaq 100, SOXX).
Unclear US policy signals that can reverse quickly.
Persistently high energy and distillate prices from the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.
vol_and_positioning: MOVE index was near its March peak while the VIX was well below its yearly average. The VIX rose Thursday and Friday but closed below 30 and below June/July levels.

JEPQ and JEPI hold about $90B combined, and QQQI, SPYI, QYLD, DIVO, GPIQ and GPIX approach another $100B. They suppress equity vol and make the VIX a weak predictor, and could drive a much bigger vol rise if they are forced to cover.
TQQQ is about $34B vs SQQQ about $2.2B, with Nasdaq 100 leveraged ETFs near $60B. SQQQ had inflows and apparent capitulation on Friday, and TQQQ saw dip buying after selling in mid-September.
SOXL is about $22B, with SOX and USD adding about $5B. NVDL holds about $4B and MUU is similar in size.
CDX trades slightly tighter than intrinsic value, and HYG, JNK, LQD, VCSH and JAAA trade near NAV. JBBB and ANGL trade at slight discounts.
Dealers are pulling back liquidity in secondary credit, per Academy's trading desk.
geopolitical: The President signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on September 18 and waived part of it on October 17, two days before the implementation deadline.

Musk joined the President's social media campaign saying Zelensky must go, and there are reports that Starlink did not work properly for Ukraine's military. Tchir says this convinced Europe its dependence on the US is fragile.
The Greenland oil Truth Social post of October 14 barely moved the oil complex.
Ongoing fighting with Iran, a Houthi-Saudi conflict, and Russia-Ukraine attacks continue. The US blockade of Iranian shipping is working.
Ukraine paused attacks on Russian refineries for a couple of days and resumed when Russia did not reciprocate.
Tchir says the President appears to be working more closely with Russia because it is positioned to act decisively.
Gulf states are reassessing their stance toward the US, Israel, Iran and the Houthis, and appear to lean toward getting back to normal rather than widening the conflict.

tension_points.bull_case: Compute-related spreads could tighten as issuance slows, and dip buying in TQQQ has been smart.
tension_points.bear_case: Wider compute spreads trigger selling in compute equities and general credit. Even if compute spreads reverse, doubts about capital access and growth keep selling going, on thin liquidity and heavy positioning.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Orderly trading in 1-2 week old new issues, where a $25 million block can be sold on the wire.
